content.p: The Hells Angels Motorcycle Club is one of the best-known outlaw motorcycle clubs. Its name turns up in rock history, in a Quebec gang war that had claimed more than 150 lives by 2000, and in court cases in Canada and the United States. Each thread below follows the order of events, and each claim is tied to the person or outlet that made it.
content.h2: The Oakland chapter and Sonny Barger
content.p: Consequence, reporting on the death of Sonny Barger in June 2022, describes him as the founder of the original Oakland chapter, which he started in 1957. The same article says the San Bernardino chapter, formed in 1947, is often credited as the first, while the Oakland chapter was the most influential. Consequence presents those two dates as a matter of record and does not explain the difference, so readers should treat the question of who came first as unsettled.

Barger was born on 8 October 1938 as Ralph Hubert Barger Jr. He became the club's most public face. According to Consequence, his gruff manner and his sayings made him one of the faces of the counterculture of the 1960s, and he also built the club's name into a commercial brand. The article says the Hells Angels name appeared on products from T-shirts to wine. Barger died at 83. A statement posted on his official Facebook page, which he had asked be published after his death, said he had passed peacefully after a brief battle with cancer.

The club's name entered the history of popular music at a free concert at Altamont Speedway in California on 6 December 1969. Consequence says about 300,000 people came to the event, which was billed as "Woodstock West," with the Rolling Stones as headliners. The Grateful Dead had been scheduled to play before the Stones but pulled out as the crowd became more violent.

The Stones had moved the concert at short notice after other venues fell through. A feature by Classical Music says the band wanted to avoid a police presence, partly because of an ongoing series of drug busts, and that it therefore asked the Hells Angels to handle security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. The same article says the club had handled security at earlier free concerts in San Francisco, including the Human Be-In of January 1967, but that the Altamont crowd was far larger and the stage was poorly prepared, with few toilets, no medical tents and little food or water.

The feature describes the violence in the crowd. It says Hells Angels fought fans during the opening sets, that Jefferson Airplane's singer Marty Balin was knocked unconscious when he tried to calm things, and that Stephen Stills of Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young was stabbed in the leg during that group's set. These are the feature's own descriptions of events, and the other reports cited here do not confirm them in detail.

The most serious incident happened during the Stones' set. The feature says Meredith Hunter, an 18-year-old from Berkeley, approached the stage, was pushed back by members hired to keep fans away, and then returned with a revolver. It says he was stabbed and beaten by Alan Passaro, a Hells Angels member. Passaro was tried in 1971 and acquitted. The feature says the jury found self-defence after viewing footage that showed Hunter drawing his gun. The footage was used in the 1970 film Gimme Shelter by Albert and David Maysles, according to the same article.

Accounts of responsibility differ. The feature reports that Jagger said the band had not known of the killing, and it quotes Barger describing the day as "just another Hells Angels event." Rolling Stone magazine, the feature says, called the concert a mix of "diabolical egotism, hype, ineptitude, money manipulation" and a lack of concern for humanity. Each of these is a judgement by a person or outlet, and none of them settles the question of blame.

In Quebec, the club's name is tied to a much darker conflict. The Christian Science Monitor, writing in September 2000, traced the war to 1994, when the Hells Angels tried to take over the rival Rock Machine while the Rock Machine's leader was in jail awaiting extradition to the United States on drug charges. The Rock Machine turned the offer down, and car bombs and shootings followed. The Monitor reported that the conflict had claimed more than 150 lives since 1994, and it quoted an opposition politician asking who was winning the war, with no convictions yet recorded.

The Monitor described the scale of the club itself in Canada. It estimated about 250 full-fledged members across the country, and 2,000 to 3,000 associates. It said the Quebec chapters behaved differently from those in western Canada, where a criminologist told the paper that members were involved in crime as individuals rather than as a chapter. The same report says an Alberta judge had ruled that a "zero tolerance" police operation against the club violated members' Charter rights.

The violence reached the press too. The Monitor reported that Michel Auger, an investigative reporter with the Journal de Montreal, was shot five times in the back in the parking lot of his newspaper. It was recovering under police guard when the paper wrote.

Quebec's response built towards the 2001 sweep. The Globe and Mail reported on 29 March 2001 that about 2,000 officers in three provinces raided clubhouses and homes before dawn. In Montreal alone, 87 suspects were due to be arraigned that day. Most members of the Nomads chapter, the Globe reported, were arrested, according to their lawyer. Among those named in the papers were Walter Stadnick and Richard Mayrand, both former national presidents of the club in Canada.

The Globe reported that the police alleged that Maurice "Mom" Boucher, already in custody awaiting trial on charges of ordering the killing of two prison guards, had masterminded the killing of at least 15 people. Police added 13 murder counts and three attempted-murder counts against him. Francis Boucher, his son, faced a murder charge tied to eight of the same deaths. The Globe reported that most of the dead were rival bikers and that one man was shot by mistake. These were allegations, and the Globe's wording reflects that.

Many of the cases from the 2001 sweep took years to reach trial. The Globe and Mail reported that Stadnick and Donald Stockford were among the last of those arrested to be tried. Both were Hamilton men and, the paper said, members of the Nomads chapter in Montreal. Stockford had been arrested at his home in Ancaster, outside Hamilton, during the 2001 operation.

In September 2004 Quebec Superior Court Justice Jerry Zigman sentenced both men to 20 years in prison. The Globe reported that a jury had found them guilty in June on five counts, among them a conspiracy to commit murder, drug trafficking and gangsterism. Stadnick had earlier been cleared of 13 murder counts and three attempted-murder counts. The Crown had asked for 24-year terms, and the defence had proposed between 13 and 15 years.

The judge called the two men violent and said they had expressed no remorse. Crown prosecutor Randall Richmond told reporters the sentences were among the heaviest given to anyone in the case. The Globe reported that 32 other Hells Angels members and associates had been convicted, and that Richmond cited 109 convictions in all. Because the two men were held for more than a decade before parole, the paper calculated that they would spend at least ten years in prison.

The Globe also reported financial evidence. Records taken from the club's drug accounts showed that in 2000 Stockford and Stadnick spent more than $11 million buying cocaine and hashish through a drug consortium called La Table. The Crown sought fines of $11 million, which the Globe said would be the largest in Canadian history, along with forfeiture of cars, cash and part of each man's home. Reports of the final financial orders were not found.

In the United States, the most significant federal case against the club's members came from Washington State. The Justice Department's Western District of Washington described it in December 2008 as the first RICO jury verdicts against an outlaw motorcycle club in twenty years. The verdicts concerned members of the club's Nomads chapter in Washington State.

The department said the case followed a ten-week trial. It reported that Rodney Rollness was sentenced to life in prison, that Joshua Binder received 15 years, and that Rick Fabel, president of the chapter, was sentenced to more than seven years. It said prosecutors had broken what it called a culture of silence and intimidation within the group. The statement was issued to recognise the trial team, so the claims about intimidation are the department's own account.

Outlaw clubs have fought each other as well as the police. In May 2015 a brawl at the Twin Peaks restaurant in Waco, Texas, left nine bikers dead. NBC News reported that the first criminal trial stemming from it ended in a mistrial in November 2017. The defendant, Christopher "Jake" Carrizal, president of the Bandidos' Dallas chapter, testified that the Cossacks had provoked the fight. Jurors deliberated for 14 hours before the judge declared a mistrial. NBC also reported that local police arrested 177 bikers after the fighting and that more than 150 people were eventually charged. The brawl was between Carrizal's group and the Cossacks. It is included here only as context for the rivalries between clubs, not as part of the Hells Angels record.

The club's history now sits between two accounts. One is the account of the courts and police, which in Quebec and Washington State produced convictions, long sentences and large financial orders. The other is the account given by the club and by its supporters, which emphasises its role as a motorcycle club and its ties to the counterculture.

The disputes that remain open are the ones the reports leave unresolved: how many people died in the Quebec war, how many members the club has in each country, who was responsible for the death at Altamont, and whether the chapters in different countries operate as one organisation. Reports from the period give different numbers and different explanations, and each one is given here with the name of the person or outlet who gave it.
